clue.text: Support troops

blocks.note: first meaning: an upright pillar holding up a structure
second meaning: a body of soldiers advancing in a long file

explanation.surface: A call to back the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a slogan backing the army; the two words are separate meanings of one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A pillar holds up a building, and a line of marching soldiers on the move is also called by this word.

clue.text: One should drive clean away from it

definitions.text: One should drive clean away from it

blocks.clueFragment: One should drive clean away from it
blocks.note: surface reading: a warning to get well clear of some danger
setter's reading: a motorist leaves a garage facility with a sparkling vehicle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clean away' reads as 'completely away'; here clean describes the car leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: An automated station where vehicles are washed by brushes and jets, after which the driver leaves with a gleaming car.

clue.text: Enticed by olden medley

indicators.note: a medley is a jumbled mixture, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lured by a collection of old songs.
explanation.definitionFit: To be led on is to be encouraged or lured into going further, often deceptively.

clue.text: Book that's dull gets cut

blocks.note: matt means without shine
to hew is to chop

explanation.surface: A boring book being edited down.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew is the first Gospel of the New Testament, one of the books of the Bible.

clue.text: Tracts of eastern and southern states

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for eastern
S is the standard abbreviation for southern
to state something is to say it, as a verb

explanation.surface: Stretches of land in the eastern and southern parts of a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tracts' looks like areas of land and 'states' like regions; tracts are really written pieces, and states is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A tract is a short written treatise or pamphlet, much like a short composition written on one subject.

clue.text: Without it, the speaker would dry up

definitions.text: Without it, the speaker would dry up

blocks.clueFragment: Without it, the speaker would dry up
blocks.note: surface reading: an orator running out of things to say
setter's reading: a talker's mouth would literally be parched

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry up' is idiom for falter in a speech; here it is literal, about the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Spit, the watery fluid produced by glands, keeps the mouth moist for talking.

clue.text: Land a hole in one - amazing start!

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: a bottomless pit or chasm
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
first letter

explanation.surface: A golfer's hole in one, an amazing start to a round.
explanation.walkthrough: Abyssinia is the old name for Ethiopia; the golf phrase 'hole in one' is split into separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Abyssinia is the former name of the African country now called Ethiopia.

clue.text: Exclude thus, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: keep someone out in this manner
setter's reading: the answer itself describes 'thus' with its letters thrown out of order, so it is one example of what it says

explanation.surface: Leaving someone out in some suggested way.
explanation.walkthrough: The second word of the answer can signal a jumble: the letters of 'thus' turned out give the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut someone out is to keep them from entering or taking part, so to bar them.

clue.text: To step on a bus is enough to change digs

blocks.clueFragment: To step on a bus is enough to change digs
blocks.note: surface reading: catching a bus is all it takes to move lodgings
setter's reading: getting on a vehicle, joined to a word for dwelling, makes the name of a kind of lodgings

explanation.surface: Moving home is as simple as hopping on a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: Digs is British slang for rented rooms; getting on a bus is the first word of the answer, and the clue jokes about turning it into lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: A private house where lodgers rent rooms and are given meals is a classic form of digs.

clue.text: Nail evil outside right

indicators.note: one word sits on the outside of another, wrapping round it

blocks.note: evil means wicked or bad
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A wicked nail sitting to the right of something.
explanation.walkthrough: BAD goes around R to make BRAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a thin small-headed wire nail used by carpenters for fine woodwork.

clue.text: People are moved by its high wire performance

definitions.text: People are moved by its high wire performance

blocks.clueFragment: People are moved by its high wire performance
blocks.note: surface reading: an audience emotionally stirred by a tightrope act at the circus
setter's reading: passengers are physically carried along by a vehicle drawing power from overhead cables

explanation.surface: A circus audience thrilled by a tightrope walker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moved' and 'high wire performance' point to the circus; the people are passengers transported by a vehicle running off overhead power lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A trolleybus is an electric bus taking its current from overhead cables via poles on the roof.

clue.text: Vessel to put to sea

blocks.note: first meaning: a large motorboat
second meaning: to set a boat afloat in the water

explanation.surface: A ship ready to set sail.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch is a type of motor boat, and to launch a ship is to send it into the water for the first time.

clue.text: The last thing those taking exams should do

definitions.text: The last thing those taking exams should do

blocks.clueFragment: The last thing those taking exams should do
blocks.note: surface reading: something examinees should avoid at all costs
setter's reading: the final activity before the papers, going back over the syllabus

explanation.surface: Advice on what students sitting exams must never do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last thing' usually means something to avoid; here it means literally the final job before the exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Going over studied material again is what students do in the days just before sitting their papers.

clue.text: Disciplinarian at Westminster requires Head to flog

blocks.note: the head of something is its chief
to flog is to lash or beat

explanation.surface: A parliamentary enforcer who needs a headmaster to do the beating.
explanation.walkthrough: Westminster is the seat of the UK Parliament; whips are the party officials who make MPs vote the party line.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief whip is the senior party official in Parliament responsible for keeping members disciplined and voting as told.

clue.text: Put a ban on spirits

blocks.note: surface reading: prohibiting alcoholic drinks
setter's reading: ghosts driven out by a priest's ritual

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' suggests drink and prohibition; here it means ghosts, banished by ritual.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive evil supernatural beings out of a person or place by prayer or ritual.

clue.text: One upper-class twit

blocks.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage
a nit is a fool, short for nitwit

explanation.surface: A single toff who is an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: U as upper-class comes from the 1950s 'U and non-U' debate on posh speech in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single thing or the number one in counting.

clue.text: Captain's favourable report on the colonel

indicators.note: in a down-reading sense one part sits on another, so the approval follows the officer here

blocks.note: a colonel commanding a regiment is its CO, commanding officer
an OK is an approving verdict

explanation.surface: A captain receives a good report about the colonel.
explanation.walkthrough: The captain is James Cook, the 18th-century naval explorer; 'on' places the approving word after the officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain James Cook was the famous British naval officer who charted the Pacific and eastern Australia.

clue.text: Take encouragement in comfort

blocks.note: first meaning: become less gloomy
second meaning: to console someone

explanation.surface: Finding heart in creature comforts.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to grow happier oneself and to make someone else feel happier.

clue.text: Not knowing or caring one is bad

indicators.note: something that has gone bad is spoilt, so the letters before it are broken up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A moral judgement that being unaware or uncaring is wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorance is the state of lacking information or awareness about something.

clue.text: Where office work is seen to be done

definitions.text: Where office work is seen to be done

blocks.clueFragment: Where office work is seen to be done
blocks.note: surface reading: the place an employee's labour is visible
setter's reading: finished papers are left on a desk tray to be collected

explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen to be done' sounds like visibly working; it means papers that are finished.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk container holding completed papers waiting to be sent on.

clue.text: Use this and all's well, presumably

definitions.text: Use this and all's well, presumably

blocks.clueFragment: Use this and all's well, presumably
blocks.note: surface reading: some trick that makes everything turn out fine
setter's reading: every patient becomes healthy after taking it

explanation.walkthrough: 'All's well' echoes the proverb; well here means healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea, a remedy claimed to treat every illness.

clue.text: Descending line in melody

blocks.note: first meaning: a breed or lineage
second meaning: a tune

explanation.surface: A falling phrase in a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Descending line' sounds musical; it is a family line of descent.
explanation.definitionFit: A strain is a line of ancestry within a breed, and also a passage of music.

clue.text: Shakespearian character to sort out crime

indicators.note: to sort things is to rearrange them into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A detective from Shakespeare who solves a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort out' looks like one phrasal verb; 'out' belongs with crime as letters, and 'sort' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercutio is Romeo's witty friend in Romeo and Juliet, killed by Tybalt.

clue.text: Drunken repast comes to a fine end

indicators.note: a drunken thing staggers about out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boozy meal that ends nicely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' means thin or narrow here, not pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that tapers narrows gradually until it ends in a thin point.

clue.text: Sound like fruit?

indicators.note: the answer is said like the next word, matching it when spoken

blocks.note: a stone fruit, pronounced identically to the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' here is the verb meaning measure the depth of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To plumb or sound is to measure water depth with a weighted line.

clue.text: He has no right to be on land

definitions.text: He has no right to be on land

blocks.clueFragment: He has no right to be on land
blocks.note: surface reading: a sailor or fish with no business ashore
setter's reading: someone on private ground without permission

explanation.surface: A sailor who should not be ashore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On land' suggests the opposite of at sea; it means on someone else's property.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who enters private property without permission commits an unlawful intrusion.

clue.text: State university backed capital investment

indicators.note: something backed is put into reverse, read from the rear

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university
a hat is something one invests in for the head, capital meaning of the head

explanation.surface: A national university financially supported by capital investment.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital is read as 'of the head' (Latin caput), so a capital investment is headwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is a western US state, home of Salt Lake City.

clue.text: The know-all gets chap in a temper

indicators.note: one item placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: to be in a pet is to be in a sulky temper
Dan is a man's name, a typical chap

explanation.surface: A smart alec makes a man furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a pet' is an old British phrase for being in a sulk, so pet serves as temper; 'a' belongs with it, not to the know-all.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant is someone fussily insistent on showing off minor points of learning or correctness.

clue.text: Sign of status?

blocks.note: surface reading: some indication of a person's standing
setter's reading: a mark that stands for something, as in the stock phrase for a prestige possession

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark nods to the phrase 'status ___', a possession that shows off wealth or rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign or emblem that represents something else, completing the familiar phrase for a prestige item.
